However, while raw speed metrics dominate benchmarks, a more insidious and pervasive problem plagues production AI systems: unpredictable latency. A model might boast incredible average inference times, but those frustrating 99th percentile (P99) or 99.9th percentile (P999) tail latencies can cripple user experience, violate critical Service Level Objectives (SLOs), and lead to massive operational inefficiencies. In real-world AI deployments, peak speed often masks a deeper issue of jitter and non-determinism, particularly under variable load or with large batch sizes. entry.title: What I Learnt From My First Go Project: Go Reloaded
entry.summary:
When I first started learning Go, I thought I understood the language. What Go Reloaded Was The Moment I Got Humbled it was the best of Times , it was the worst of TIMES,
whereas the expected output was: It was the best of times, it was the worst of TIMES,
One tiny comma. One small space. And the test failed. It was frustrating, but it taught me something crucial: precision matters. Computers don’t guess what you meant — they only care what you actually wrote. What I Learned This project set the tone for all my future Go work. After Go Reloaded: Go Reloaded was more than just code — it was my first taste of learning in public. Final Thought Sometimes the smallest projects teach the biggest lessons. Go Reloaded taught me to slow down, pay attention, and embrace the little mistakes because that’s where growth happens.

entry.title: Bias You Can Notice vs Bias You Can’t
entry.summary: While generating exam questions with generative AI, I noticed a subtle pattern: the correct answer almost never appeared in position (a). The content was fine. The bias was procedural — and invisible until I knew where to look. This essay explores the difference between bias we can notice and bias we can’t, and why the most dangerous biases aren’t ideological or malicious. They’re structural, normalized, and easy to miss — especially in systems that move quickly, confidently, and without looking back.

entry.title: Linux Fundamentals - Part 9: Bash Scripting (Arrays)
entry.summary:
Bash Arrays
A Bash array is a variable that can hold multiple values, each stored at a specific index. Instead of creating many separate variables, arrays let us group related data together. Example use cases: List of servers Packages to install Users to create Files or directories to process servers=("web1" "web2" "web")
Each value is separated by a space and wrapped in parentheses. You can also create arrays like this: servers[1]="web1" servers[2]="web2" servers[3]="web3"
To access an element, use its index: echo ${servers[0]}
Output: web1
Always use ${} when accessing array values.
